A1.justification: Both PDFs describe QueryOcc by the same authors. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete supplementary material are readable and support reliable matching across relocations and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original occupancy-prediction experiments, runtime measurements, component ablations, dataset-scaling experiments, and qualitative results in the main text and supplement.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds results on supervision noise, contraction sensitivity, component combinations, and lidar-point semantic segmentation.

M1.justification: The lift-contract-splat architecture, spatial contraction, query decoder, query generation, and training objectives are unchanged. Additional ablation settings do not revise the proposed method; the point-encoding equation is merely moved inline.

E1.justification: Section 9.11 adds evaluation of semantic predictions at lidar-point locations against Panoptic nuScenes annotations, extending evaluation beyond voxel occupancy. This is a related task within the existing driving domain. nuScenes, Argoverse 2, and nuPlan were already used in v1; the original dataset-mixture experiment remains in v2 Table 17.

E2.justification: The occupancy benchmark comparators remain unchanged, including GaussianFlowOcc and both GaussTR variants. The new lidar-segmentation comparison directly evaluates projected pseudo-label predictions against QueryOcc in Tables 18–19 and Figure 10, adding a comparator for that evaluation.

E3.justification: New experimental protocols inject Gaussian noise into predicted inverse depth and randomly flip semantic labels, vary dnear and Khr over 10–40 m, and evaluate lidar-point predictions using IoU, recall, F1, and accuracy. The existing occupancy evaluation and core training settings remain unchanged. Newly explained controls for existing component ablations are documentation additions, not established protocol revisions.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands validation through controlled supervision-noise tests, contraction-range sensitivity, two additional component combinations in Table 4, and an analysis of whether QueryOcc improves on its pseudo-label supervision, including class-wise errors and confusion matrices. These address robustness and denoising questions not directly tested in v1. The temporal-window study is retained through relocation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates for experimental scores. The added random-noise experiments test robustness rather than introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Substantive new results quantify noise degradation, contraction sensitivity, and pseudo-label refinement: semantic RayIoU reaches 19.2 under the strongest joint corruption, spans 23.4–23.7 across contraction ranges, and lidar-segmentation mean IoU is 49.8 for QueryOcc versus 35.5 for pseudo-labels. New Table 6 reports 26.0/23.8/50.8 for nuScenes+AV2. The earlier 24.3/20.8/50.5 result remains in Table 17 under its VFM-supervision description, so this is not an established same-setting improvement. Main benchmark scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulations are unchanged, including spatial contraction, query sampling, losses, and rendering. Equation renumbering and moving point encoding inline introduce no new definitions, derivations, assumptions, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about direct 4D supervision, unbounded contracted representation, flexible supervision, scalability, and state-of-the-art occupancy prediction. The headline 26% semantic RayIoU advantage and 11.6 FPS claim are unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning robustness to noisy supervision, information preservation across contraction settings, and denoising beyond pseudo-label quality. Section 9.10 attributes scaling saturation partly to weaker VFM supervision, while Section 9.11 acknowledges trailer underperformance and persistent truck/trailer confusion. The original occlusion limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 4.3 newly explains fixed BEV cell counts, exclusion of queries beyond 40 m in short-range ablations, and boundary mapping without contraction. v2 removes the prospective open-source-code statement from Section 3.3, while retaining the project-page link and core implementation, training, and hardware details. This does not establish any change in actual code availability.

R1.justification: The same 44 cited works and research positioning are retained. GASP and MinkOcc receive publication-metadata updates rather than being replaced by different works. Panoptic nuScenes was already cited in v1.

P1.justification: v2 makes limited wording edits, expands the component-ablation explanation, and adds supplementary subsections. The temporal-window discussion moves from Section 4.3 to Section 9.6, and the original dataset-scaling discussion moves to Section 9.10 with revisions. The overall narrative and principal sections remain stable.

P2.justification: Table 4 gains rows, and new tables and paired confusion matrices display the additional experiments. Original Table 6 becomes Table 17, while temporal-window Figure 5 becomes supplementary Figure 8. Other plots are repositioned, but the architecture diagrams and five qualitative scene examples retain their content. These are localized additions and layout adjustments.

improvement.justification: The added noise tests, contraction sensitivity, and direct comparison against pseudo-labels strengthen evidence that QueryOcc learns useful representations from imperfect supervision. Clarified ablation controls also improve interpretability. These are incremental gains over v1's retained method and benchmark evidence. Brief specification of the new AV2 supervision comparison and removal of the prospective code-release statement temper, but do not outweigh, the improvement.
